title: Adaptive Warmup Interval and Staleness Tuning — Cycle 23 Closure
summary: Closed Cycle 23 by adding an adaptive layer on top of the Cycle 22 predictive warmup cache/scheduler. A new WarmupVolatilityTracker actor records per-(provider, baseURL, model) success/failure outcomes and recommends TTL and scheduler interval based on recent failure rate. PredictiveWarmupCache now supports per-record TTL and remaining-ttl queries; PredictiveWarmupScheduler can restart with a new interval at runtime. ModelConfigurationStore owns the published TTL/interval settings (persisted to UserDefaults) and runs an adaptive warmup cadence. ChatViewModel records real send outcomes back into the volatility tracker. UI steppers and cache-freshness/failure-rate badges were added to ModelsTabView. All Trinity gates passed and trios.app relaunched with the logo present.
learnings: Adaptive TTL should be driven by actual observed outcomes, not by static configuration, or the cache will expire many times before the next scheduled refresh.
A bounded rolling window per candidate keeps memory use constant and lets the system respond to recent volatility without overreacting to ancient failures.
Restarting the scheduler with a new interval is safer when it first stops the old Task cleanly and resets the sleep boundary.
Closing the feedback loop in ChatViewModel (recording whether the cached winner succeeded or failed) is what makes the volatility tracker useful; otherwise it stays at zero forever.
UI controls need immediate SwiftUI .onChange handlers that persist to UserDefaults; published defaults must be loaded from UserDefaults at init to avoid resetting on every cold start.
remaining_weak_spots: Volatility history is in-memory only; app restarts reset the tracker.
Chat still waits synchronously if no fresh cached winner exists; stale-while-revalidate is not implemented.
There is no per-conversation provider/model pinning; adaptive suggestions may propose a model the user did not intend for a given thread.
